strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use a full-covariance CMA-ES search in an orthonormal coordinate system for the fixed-sum constraint. Each Gaussian sample is decoded to h and jointly projected onto the box-and-sum feasible set; its fitness is the exact finite linear-correlation score. Keep the supplied construction as the initial center and a protected fallback whenever it is usable.

This is substantively different from an epigraph solve, projected-gradient smoothing, pair-transfer search, and differential evolution. It uses neither gradients nor pairwise coordinate moves, differential donors, or crossover. Its search distribution learns correlated directions through rank-one and rank-mu covariance updates and cumulative step-size adaptation. Eliminating the sum direction before sampling also avoids spending search effort on infeasible changes in total mass.

The justified facts are that the evaluator uses all 2N-1 finite lags, the box-and-sum set is convex, and products of entries of h make the objective generally nonconvex. CMA-ES is a derivative-free local/global heuristic, not a convex solver or a certificate of global optimality. The hypothesis is that learning correlations among sample coordinates and restarting around the best exact candidate may find improvements that local gradient or coordinate searches miss. Projection can distort Gaussian samples, finite runs can stagnate, and no score improvement or target bound is guaranteed. Return only the best feasible candidate actually found by the executed program.

2. Mathematical specification

Let N be the runtime sample count, dx=2/N, and m=N/2. The feasible set is K={h in R^N: 0<=h_i<=1 for every i and sum_i h_i=m}. For each integer lag s from -(N-1) through N-1, define
q_s(h)=sum_{i=max(0,-s)}^{min(N-1,N-1-s)} h_i*(1-h_(i+s)).
These are finite-overlap sums: do not wrap indices or add missing boundary terms. The q_s values are exactly the 2N-1 values of the full linear correlation, possibly in reversed lag order. The authoritative objective is
C(h)=(2/N)*max_s q_s(h)=max(np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full'))*(2.0/N).
Minimize C over K. Do not replace it with circular correlation or an autocorrelation identity that omits boundary terms.

For N>=2, set u=0.5*ones(N) and d=N-1. Build an N-by-d matrix B with columns indexed k=0,...,N-2. For column k, let a=sqrt((k+1)*(k+2)); set B[i,k]=1/a for i=0,...,k, B[k+1,k]=-(k+1)/a, and all other entries in that column to zero. Then B.T@B=I and B.T@ones(N)=0. Every vector in the affine sum hyperplane has a unique coordinate x=B.T@(h-u), with h=u+B@x. The feasible coordinate domain is X={x: u+B@x is in K}.

Decode an arbitrary search coordinate x_raw by computing z=u+B@x_raw, projecting z onto K, and then setting x_repaired=B.T@(h-u). This is Euclidean projection in the reduced coordinates too, because B is an isometry from R^d onto the zero-sum subspace. Thus every decoded candidate satisfies the sum and box constraints jointly. The CMA mean will be maintained as a convex combination of repaired feasible coordinates, and therefore also represents a feasible point up to floating-point roundoff.

For any z, the Euclidean projection onto K has entries P_K(z)_i=clip(z_i-lambda,0,1), where lambda is chosen so that sum_i clip(z_i-lambda,0,1)=m. The left side is continuous and nonincreasing in lambda. Bisection between min(z)-1 and max(z) brackets a root; a deterministic residual correction using only available box slack removes the remaining floating-point sum error. Clipping followed by rescaling is not a valid substitute.

CMA-ES maintains a mean mu in R^d, a positive-definite covariance matrix C, and a positive step size sigma. Given C=Q diag(D) Q.T, sample z_j from a standard normal in R^d and form y_j=Q diag(sqrt(D)) z_j and x_raw,j=mu+sigma*y_j. Decode and exactly score each candidate. Rank candidates by their exact scores; the best mu_sel candidates determine positive recombination weights. The algorithm updates the mean from their repaired coordinates, the covariance from their normalized repaired steps, and the step size from cumulative evolution paths. These are rank-based heuristic updates for the nonconvex exact objective; no differentiability or convexity claim is made.

For completeness, let lambda_pop be the population size, mu_sel=floor(lambda_pop/2), and for one-based i=1,...,mu_sel let w_i be proportional to ln(mu_sel+0.5)-ln(i), normalized to sum to one. Define mu_eff=1/sum_i w_i^2. For dimension d use
c_sigma=(mu_eff+2)/(d+mu_eff+5),
d_sigma=1+2*max(0,sqrt((mu_eff-1)/(d+1))-1)+c_sigma,
c_c=(4+mu_eff/d)/(d+4+2*mu_eff/d),
c1=2/((d+1.3)^2+mu_eff),
c_mu=min(1-c1, 2*(mu_eff-2+1/mu_eff)/((d+2)^2+mu_eff)),
and chi_d=sqrt(d)*(1-1/(4*d)+1/(21*d*d)). With old mean mu, repaired selected coordinates x_i, and old sigma, set y_i=(x_i-mu)/sigma and y_w=(mu_new-mu)/sigma, where mu_new is their weighted mean after numerical feasibility restoration. Update
p_sigma=(1-c_sigma)*p_sigma+sqrt(c_sigma*(2-c_sigma)*mu_eff)*C^(-1/2)@y_w.
At local generation t, set h_sigma=1 if norm(p_sigma)/sqrt(1-(1-c_sigma)^(2*t)) < (1.4+2/(d+1))*chi_d, and otherwise set it to 0. Update
p_c=(1-c_c)*p_c+h_sigma*sqrt(c_c*(2-c_c)*mu_eff)*y_w,
C_new=(1-c1-c_mu)*C+c1*(p_c@p_c.T+(1-h_sigma)*c_c*(2-c_c)*C)+c_mu*sum_i w_i*(y_i@y_i.T),
sigma_new=sigma*exp((c_sigma/d_sigma)*(norm(p_sigma)/chi_d-1)).
Here each y_i@y_i.T denotes an outer product. Use only positive recombination weights. Section 3 specifies how to apply these equations to projected samples and handle numerical failures.

3. Implementation procedure

1. Write one complete program defining run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level. Put every helper at top level; do not use closures or lambdas. Use float64 NumPy arrays and math as needed. NumPy linear algebra is sufficient; no solver, filesystem or network access, parallel execution, or progress printing is needed. Do not redefine evaluate_erdos_solution or initial_h_values, and do not copy or embed parent entries. Implement the exact score internally.

2. Initialize one NumPy Generator with np.random.default_rng(seed); if that raises an exception, retry with seed 42. Read the optional parent using globals().get('initial_h_values', None) and attempt float64 conversion. A finite, one-dimensional, nonempty parent determines N from its full length; never truncate, interpolate, or change that resolution. If it is already feasible, use a copy directly as the baseline and CMA center. If finite but outside the constraints, project it with the joint projector and use the projected result as the baseline and center. If projection fails, use the uniform vector of that parent-derived length. A malformed, empty, multidimensional, or nonfinite parent is unavailable. Without a usable parent, accept kwargs.get('n_points',70) only when it is an integer or NumPy integer, not a Boolean, and lies in [1,999]; otherwise set N=70. Use the uniform vector as the no-parent baseline. Set m=N/2 in every case.

3. Implement top-level feasibility, projection, decoding, and scoring helpers. The feasibility helper requires shape (N,), finite values, bounds within 1e-12 of [0,1], and abs(sum(h)-m)<=1e-10*max(1,N). The projection helper accepts a length-N finite vector; otherwise return the uniform feasible vector. To avoid overflow, reject inputs with absolute entries above 1e100 to the uniform fallback, subtract the median from otherwise valid inputs (this leaves the projection unchanged), and bracket lambda using low=min(z)-1 and high=max(z). Perform 100 bisection iterations, using mid=low+(high-low)/2; if sum(clip(z-mid,0,1))>m, set low=mid, otherwise set high=mid. Form h using the final midpoint. Correct r=m-sum(h) deterministically in index order: for positive r, add at most 1-h_i; for negative r, subtract at most h_i. Recompute the residual and make a second pass if necessary. Return h only if it is finite, within bounds, and passes the sum tolerance; otherwise return the uniform vector. Do not clip or rescale a projected candidate in a way that loses its sum.

The exact-score helper rejects wrong shape or nonfinite input with positive infinity. Otherwise compute corr=np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full'), reject nonfinite correlation values, and return float(np.max(corr)*(2.0/N)). This call evaluates all 2N-1 finite lags in the evaluator's linear-correlation convention. Never score a candidate using a surrogate.

4. Build the Helmert basis B from section 2 only when search is enabled. Use shape (N,N-1), and return without search when N=1. Define u=0.5*ones(N). Convert a feasible h to coordinates by B.T@(h-u). To decode x, reject nonfinite coordinates, form z=u+B@x, project z with the joint projector, validate the resulting h, and return both h and B.T@(h-u). Keep the exact projected h as the candidate; the coordinates are for CMA updates. A decode failure rejects that sample rather than replacing the global best.

5. Initialize a CMA run at the current global best: mu=B.T@(best_h-u), C=I_d, p_sigma=0, p_c=0, and sigma equal to the tier-specific value in section 4. Use lambda_pop=max(4,4+floor(3*ln(d))) and mu_sel=floor(lambda_pop/2). Compute the positive weights and CMA constants exactly as specified in section 2. Set local generation count and stagnation count to zero for each run. The global best and its exact score persist across runs; each restart initializes fresh identity covariance and zero paths but centers at the current global best.

6. At each generation, symmetrize C and obtain its eigendecomposition with np.linalg.eigh. Clip eigenvalues to [max(1e-12, largest_eigenvalue*1e-10), 1e4], reconstruct the regularized C, and use the same eigenvectors and clipped eigenvalues to form Q diag(sqrt(D)) and C^(-1/2)=Q diag(1/sqrt(D)) Q.T. Draw lambda_pop independent standard-normal vectors, form the raw coordinates from the CMA sampling formula, decode each, and compute its exact score only after feasibility validation. Keep arrays of repaired coordinates, vectors, and scores of size lambda_pop. If an individual sample is nonfinite or cannot be decoded, substitute the current feasible mean point as that sample; it is a valid duplicate, not a new improvement. Compare every valid sample to the global best and store a copy only when its exact score is lower by more than 1e-12. Rank this generation's candidates by exact score using a stable sort so ties have deterministic ordering. CMA selection is based on this generation only; do not use differential donors, coordinate crossover, or greedy per-coordinate replacement.

7. For the best mu_sel ranked samples, compute y_i=(x_i-mu_old)/sigma. Compute their weighted coordinate mean. Reconstruct h_mean=u+B@mu_new, project it jointly for numerical safety, validate it, and reset mu_new=B.T@(h_mean-u). Define y_w=(mu_new-mu_old)/sigma. Evaluate h_mean with the exact score and let it update the global best if it beats it by more than 1e-12. Use the old C and its inverse square root for the path updates. Apply the p_sigma and h_sigma formulas in section 2, with t=local_generation+1, then update p_c and C using the selected repaired steps y_i and the stated rank-one plus rank-mu formula. Symmetrize the result. Update sigma with the stated exponential formula, but clamp its exponent to [-1,1] and clamp sigma to [1e-4,0.5]. All selections, path updates, covariance updates, and candidate comparisons use float64 values and reject nonfinite intermediates.

At the beginning of a generation save the current global-best score. After scoring samples and the updated mean, reset the stagnation counter if the global best improved by more than 1e-12; otherwise increment it. Stop the current CMA run if its generation limit is reached, the counter reaches its tier limit, sigma is at most 1e-4, or the covariance cannot be recovered under the safeguards in section 5. A run ending without improvement still leaves its best feasible candidates available for the next restart.

8. Run the tier-specified number of CMA runs in order. The first is centered at the baseline. Each later run is centered at the current global best and uses its tier's smaller restart sigma, with fresh C=I and reset evolution paths. The random generator continues from its seeded state; do not recreate it between runs. Every candidate and every mean evaluation is handled inside the program. If a run raises an exception, terminate that run while preserving the best candidate and continue to the next configured restart when possible. If no search is enabled, retain the baseline and do not allocate B or C.

9. Before returning, independently project the stored global best and the original feasible baseline, validate both, and recompute both exact scores. Select the search result only if it has a finite score and improves on the recomputed baseline by more than 1e-12; otherwise retain the baseline. Project and validate the selected vector once more and recompute its exact score. If any final check or score fails, use the feasible baseline; if that also fails, use h=0.5*ones(N). Recompute the score of whichever vector is actually returned.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use these defaults without preliminary experiments. For N=1, skip search. For 2<=N<=96, use three CMA runs with at most 100 generations per run, a stagnation limit of 24 generations, and initial sigmas [0.12, 0.07, 0.035]. For 97<=N<=160, use two runs, at most 60 generations per run, a stagnation limit of 18, and sigmas [0.10, 0.05]. For 161<=N<=256, use one run, at most 30 generations, a stagnation limit of 12, and sigma 0.08. For N>256, retain and exactly score the validated baseline but skip full-covariance search to bound eigen-decomposition cost and memory. The supplied 70-sample parent uses the first tier. The population size in every searched tier is max(4,4+floor(3*ln(N-1))). The generation cap applies separately to each run; stagnation can end a run sooner.

Keep the default score-improvement threshold at 1e-12, covariance regularization, projection, and exact-score comparison unchanged. Reasonable bounded variations are sigma starts in [0.05,0.20], one to four runs for N<=96, 40-140 generations for the small tier, and proportionally fewer generations in larger tiers. A coder may use these variations for implementation reasons without external measurements. Any result-dependent action must be explicit code behavior, such as the specified stagnation stop or re-centering a restart at the current global best. Correctness requirements do not vary: preserve N, include every finite lag in the exact score, enforce box and sum jointly, and preserve the baseline fallback. The target 0.3808 is not an acceptance threshold or a promised result.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 throughout and validate all inputs, decoded candidates, means, scores, paths, eigenvalues, and covariance updates. Projection rejects nonfinite or extreme inputs to the uniform feasible vector and verifies its residual correction. Search samples that are invalid are rejected or replaced only by the current feasible mean as a duplicate; they never overwrite a valid incumbent. The exact-score helper returns infinity on invalid input or nonfinite correlation, and such a score is never accepted.

Symmetrize C before eigendecomposition and after each update. Use the eigenvalue floor and cap specified in section 3. If an eigendecomposition or covariance update is nonfinite or fails, reset C to identity and both paths to zero, halve sigma subject to its lower bound, and retry at most once in that run. If recovery fails again, stop that run. Clamp the step-size exponent and sigma as specified. A failed run or a run with no improvement preserves the global best and the original baseline. No generic solver failure path is needed because the program uses no external optimizer.

The exact correlation needs a length-(2N-1) result and O(N^2) work per score. A searched run stores B of size N by N-1, C and eigensystem arrays of size (N-1) by (N-1), and a population of lambda_pop length-N vectors; the memory is O(N^2+lambda_pop*N). At the search cap N=256 these dense arrays are modest. Covariance eigendecomposition is O(N^3), which is why full-covariance search is disabled above that cap. Do not build a dense lag-by-coordinate Jacobian, Hessian, or table of pairwise products. Use the single available CPU; do not parallelize evaluations. If all runs fail or produce no improvement, return the protected baseline rather than an unverified proposal.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated program itself must read and validate the optional parent, derive N from a usable finite one-dimensional parent, otherwise validate kwargs.get('n_points',70) and apply the specified fallback. Never hard-code parent samples. Every scored or stored candidate must have shape (N,), finite entries, bounds within tolerance, and sum within the stated tolerance; use the joint projection for sample decoding and final restoration. Keep the baseline available regardless of all CMA updates and restarts.

Implement the returned score internally as float(np.max(np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full'))*(2.0/N)) after validating h. Use this exact full finite correlation for baseline scoring, all candidate ranking, best-candidate storage, final selection, and c5_bound. Do not use a surrogate, omit lags, or assume a target score has been reached. On any search or final-validation failure, select the feasible baseline, or the uniform vector if no valid baseline remains, and recompute its exact score. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), where h_values is a one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, c5_bound is a Python float, and n_points is int(N). Produce no other output.
